blocks.text: A function \(f\) is one-to-one if different inputs produce different outputs, i.e., if \(f(x_{1}) = f(x_{2})\) implies \(x_{1} = x_{2}\). This means that no two different elements of the domain map to the same element of the co-domain.
For example, \(f(x) = 5x + 7\) is one-to-one because \(5x_{1} + 7 = 5x_{2} + 7\) implies \(x_{1} = x_{2}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The missing small steps in the book's example: subtract \(7\) from both sides, then divide by \(5\):
\[5x_{1} + 7 = 5x_{2} + 7\]
\[5x_{1} = 5x_{2}\]
\[x_{1} = x_{2}\]
Method to prove one-to-one: assume \(f(x_{1}) = f(x_{2})\) and show by algebra that \(x_{1} = x_{2}\).
Method to disprove: find two different inputs with the same output (one counter-example is enough).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: On a graph, one-to-one can be checked with a horizontal line: a function is one-to-one if no horizontal line meets its graph more than once. (Compare the vertical line test of 2.1.3, which checks whether a graph is a function at all.)

A function \(f : X \to Y\) is called an onto (or surjective) function if every element in the co-domain \(Y\) has at least one pre-image in the domain \(X\). In other words, for every \(y\) in \(Y\), there exists an \(x\) in \(X\) such that \(f(x) = y\).

For example, \(f(x) = 2x + 3\), where the domain and co-domain are both the real numbers. Here
\[y = 2x + 3\]
\[\Rightarrow x = \dfrac{y - 3}{2}\]
\[f\left(\dfrac{y - 3}{2}\right) = 2\left(\dfrac{y - 3}{2}\right) + 3 = y\]
For each \(y\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) there exists \(\frac{y - 3}{2}\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) such that \(f\left(\frac{y - 3}{2}\right) = y\). Hence \(f\) is an onto function.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A pre-image of \(y\) is an input \(x\) whose output is \(y\). Onto means: range = co-domain (no element of the co-domain is left unused).
Method to prove onto: take any \(y\) in the co-domain, solve \(y = f(x)\) for \(x\), check that this \(x\) is in the domain, and verify \(f(x) = y\).
Onto depends on the co-domain chosen: \(f(x) = x^{2}\) from \(\mathbb{R}\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) is not onto (\(-1\) has no pre-image), but from \(\mathbb{R}\) to \([0, \infty)\) it is onto.
A function \(f : X \to Y\) is called bijective if it is both one-to-one and onto.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Bijective means a perfect pairing: every element of \(Y\) is the output of exactly one element of \(X\) (onto gives "at least one", one-to-one gives "at most one"). To prove bijective, prove both parts separately. The functions \(5x + 7\) and \(2x + 3\) above are both bijective from \(\mathbb{R}\) to \(\mathbb{R}\).

blocks.text: A piecewise function is a function that is defined by different expressions (or "pieces") over different intervals of its domain. Each piece applies to a specific part of the domain.

blocks.text_alt: f of x equals 2 x plus 1 if x is less than 0, and x squared minus 1 if x is greater than or equal to 0

blocks.text: For \(x < 0\), the function behaves like \(2x + 1\) and for \(x \ge 0\), it behaves like \(x^{2} - 1\).

blocks.alt: Graph on a grid from minus 4 to 4 on the x-axis and minus 3 to 3 on the y-axis. For x less than 0 a straight line y = 2x + 1 rises from (minus 2, minus 3) to an open circle at (0, 1). For x greater than or equal to 0 the curve y = x squared minus 1 starts at a filled dot (0, minus 1), crosses the x-axis at (1, 0) and rises to (2, 3).
blocks.caption: Figure: the piecewise function f(x) = 2x + 1 for x < 0 and x² − 1 for x ≥ 0 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
To evaluate a piecewise function, first decide which piece the input belongs to, then use only that piece:
\(f(-2)\): \(-2 < 0\), so \(f(-2) = 2(-2) + 1 = -3\).
\(f(0)\): \(0 \ge 0\), so \(f(0) = 0^{2} - 1 = -1\).
\(f(2)\): \(2 \ge 0\), so \(f(2) = 2^{2} - 1 = 3\).
On the graph, the line stops just before \(x = 0\): the open circle at \((0, 1)\) shows that point is not on the graph; the filled dot at \((0, -1)\) shows that \(f(0) = -1\). Each input still has only one output, so a piecewise function is a genuine function.

blocks.title: Example 5
blocks.problem: Show that the function \(f(x) = x + 1\), where the domain and co-domain are all real numbers, is bijective.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x + 1\), \(f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\).
To prove: \(f\) is bijective.
Method: a function is bijective if it is both one-to-one and onto, so prove the two parts separately.

Part 1: one-to-one
A function is one-to-one if \(f(x_{1}) = f(x_{2}) \Rightarrow x_{1} = x_{2}\). Suppose
\[f(x_{1}) = f(x_{2})\]
\[x_{1} + 1 = x_{2} + 1\]
\[\Rightarrow x_{1} = x_{2}\]
So the given function is one-to-one.
Why: subtracting \(1\) from both sides leaves \(x_{1} = x_{2}\): equal outputs can only come from equal inputs.

Part 2: onto
Take any real number \(y\). Solve \(y = x + 1\): \(x = y - 1\), which is a real number.
\[f(y - 1) = y - 1 + 1 = y\]
Why: every \(y\) in the co-domain has the pre-image \(y - 1\) in the domain, which is exactly the definition of onto.

Conclusion
\(f\) is one-to-one and onto, therefore \(f(x)\) is bijective.

Check:
Try \(y = 7\): the pre-image is \(7 - 1 = 6\), and \(f(6) = 7\). Two different inputs, e.g. \(2\) and \(5\), give \(3\) and \(6\), which are different, as one-to-one requires.
blocks.answer: Hence proved: \(f(x) = x + 1\) is one-to-one and onto, so it is bijective.

blocks.title: Example 6
blocks.problem: Show that the function \(f(x) = x^{2} - 2\), where the domain and co-domain are all real numbers, is neither one-to-one nor onto.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x^{2} - 2\), \(f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\).
To prove: \(f\) is not one-to-one and not onto.
Method: to show a property fails, one counter-example is enough. Find two inputs with the same output, and one element of the co-domain with no pre-image.

Try the one-to-one condition
\[f(x_{1}) = f(x_{2})\]
\[x_{1}^{2} - 2 = x_{2}^{2} - 2\]
\[x_{1}^{2} = x_{2}^{2}\]
Taking square root, we get \(x_{1} = x_{2}\) or \(x_{1} = -x_{2}\).
Why: two numbers have the same square when they are equal or negatives of each other, so equal outputs do not force equal inputs.

Counter-example: not one-to-one
\(x_{1} = 2\), \(x_{2} = -2\), so \(x_{1} \ne x_{2}\), and
\[f(2) = 4 - 2 = 2\]
\[f(-2) = 4 - 2 = 2\]
Thus \(f\) is not one-to-one.
Why: two different inputs give the same output \(2\) (see the dashed line at height 2 in the figure).

Not onto
\(x^{2} \ge 0\), so \(f(x) = x^{2} - 2 \ge -2\). The smallest value \(f\) can attain is \(-2\), and only when \(x = 0\).
Any number less than \(-2\) in the co-domain \(\mathbb{R}\) is not the image of any real \(x\). For example, \(f(x) = -3\):
\[x^{2} - 2 = -3\]
\[x^{2} = -1\]
which has no real root.
Why: the co-domain is all of \(\mathbb{R}\), but the range is only \([-2, \infty)\); the element \(-3\) has no pre-image.

Check:
From the graph: the horizontal line \(y = 2\) meets the parabola twice (not one-to-one), and the parabola never goes below its lowest point \((0, -2)\) (not onto).
blocks.answer: Hence proved: \(f(x) = x^{2} - 2\) is not one-to-one (\(f(2) = f(-2) = 2\)) and not onto (\(-3\) has no pre-image).

blocks.alt: Graph of the parabola y = x squared minus 2 with lowest point (0, minus 2). The points (minus 2, 2) and (2, 2) are marked and joined by a dashed horizontal line at height 2, with dashed vertical lines down to x = minus 2 and x = 2. Labels: f(minus 2) = 2 and f(2) = 2.
blocks.caption: Figure: f(x) = x² − 2 takes the same value 2 at x = −2 and x = 2 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. One-to-one: \(f(x_{1}) = f(x_{2}) \Rightarrow x_{1} = x_{2}\) (different inputs, different outputs).
2. Onto: every element of the co-domain has at least one pre-image; range = co-domain.
3. Bijective: one-to-one and onto.
4. To prove a property, use general \(x_{1}, x_{2}\) or a general \(y\); to disprove, one counter-example is enough.
5. A piecewise function uses different formulas on different parts of the domain; pick the piece first.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Proving one-to-one with numbers ("\(f(1) \ne f(2)\)"). A few examples never prove it; use general \(x_{1}, x_{2}\).
2. Forgetting to check that the pre-image lies in the domain when proving onto.
3. Saying a function is onto without looking at the co-domain: \(x^{2}\) is onto \([0, \infty)\) but not onto \(\mathbb{R}\).
4. In a piecewise function, using both pieces for one input, or the wrong piece at the boundary \(x = 0\).
